<reason>CON (A) built a coherent, escalating case that the metric PRO relies on (cost-per-contact, containment, repeat-contact rate) is structurally blind to the harms it needs to measure — silent churn, hallucinated-policy liability, and misrouted high-stakes contacts. This "the ledger can't see its own losses" framing, crystallized in A4.4 and the closing, was never squarely answered: PRO's response that "repeat-contact metrics already exist" addresses within-channel repeats, not full customer churn to a competitor, and PRO never returned to close that gap. PRO (B) landed real points — Air Canada shows accountability rather than its absence, human baselines are also flawed, and CON never supplied a comparative number — but its central weapon ("CON gave no figures") cuts both ways, since PRO's own "structural and certain" savings claim was equally unquantified, and CON exploited that symmetry cleanly in rebuttal 2 and closing. Both sides handled the Pressure Questions format correctly (A1/A2 labels present), but CON's answers (especially the apprenticeship/pipeline mechanism and the churn-vs-repeat-contact distinction) were more substantive than PRO's largely qualitative rejoinders. PRO's opening was also clipped for length, a real execution cost. Overall CON gave the cleaner, more original reason to distrust PRO's own accounting, which PRO never fully neutralized.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's argument that repeat-contact tracking cannot see full customer churn ("silent churn is invisible to the very dashboards PRO trusts," A4.4), answering PRO's claim that existing metrics already capture the "customer gave up" signal (B4.1) — this exchange most directly determined whether either side's cost ledger could be trusted.</best_rebuttal>
